title: Chapter 7. Of the Ends or Resolutions of Discourse
paragraphs: All discourse governed by the desire of knowledge comes to an end at last, either by attaining what was sought, or by giving up. And in the chain of discourse, wherever it is interrupted, there is an end for that time.

If the discourse is purely mental, it consists of thoughts alternating between the thing will be and will not be, or has been and has not been. So wherever you break off the chain of a man's discourse, you leave him in a presumption that 'It will be' or 'It will not be,' or 'It has been' or 'It has not been' — all of which is opinion. And what, in deliberating about good and evil, is alternate appetite, is the same as alternate opinion in the inquiry into the truth of the past and the future. Just as the last appetite in deliberation is called the will, so the last opinion in the search for the truth of the past and the future is called the JUDGEMENT, or the resolute and final verdict of the man whose discourse it is. And just as the whole chain of alternating appetites, on the question of good or bad, is called deliberation, so the whole chain of alternating opinions, on the question of true or false, is called DOUBT.

No discourse whatsoever can end in absolute knowledge of fact, past or future. For as for the knowledge of fact, it is originally sense, and ever after memory. And as for the knowledge of consequence, which I said before is called science, it is not absolute but conditional. No man can know by discourse that this or that is, has been, or will be — which would be to know absolutely. He can only know that if this is, that is; if this has been, that has been; if this shall be, that shall be — which is to know conditionally; and not the consequence of one thing to another, but the consequence of one name of a thing to another name of the same thing.

And so when discourse is put into speech, and begins with the definitions of words, and proceeds by the connection of those into general affirmations, and from those again into syllogisms, the end or final sum is called the conclusion; and the thought of the mind signified by it is the conditional knowledge, or knowledge of the consequence of words, that is commonly called science. But if the first ground of such discourse is not definitions, or if the definitions are not rightly joined together into syllogisms, then the end or conclusion is again opinion — namely, opinion about the truth of something said, even if sometimes in absurd and senseless words, beyond any possibility of being understood. When two or more men know of one and the same fact, they are said to be CONSCIOUS of it with one another — that is, to know it together. And because such men are the fittest witnesses of one another's actions, or of the actions of a third party, it has always been, and ever will be, considered a very evil act for a man to speak against his conscience, or to corrupt or force another into doing so. So much so that the plea of conscience has always been listened to with great diligence in every age. Later, men used the same word metaphorically for the knowledge of their own secret acts and secret thoughts, and so it is said rhetorically that conscience is a thousand witnesses. And last of all, men vehemently in love with their own novel opinions (however absurd), and stubbornly bent on maintaining them, gave those opinions of theirs also the reverent name of conscience — as if they wanted to make it unlawful to change or speak against them — and so pretend to know their opinions are true, when at most they know only that they think so.

When a man's discourse does not begin at definitions, it begins either at some other reflection of his own — and then it is still called opinion — or at some saying of another whose ability to know the truth and whose honesty in not deceiving he does not doubt; and then the discourse is not so much about the thing as about the person. The resolution of this is called BELIEF, and FAITH: faith, in the man; belief, both of the man and of the truth of what he says. So in belief there are two opinions: one of the man's saying, the other of his virtue. 'To have faith in,' 'to trust to,' and 'to believe a man' all mean the same thing — an opinion of the man's truthfulness. But 'to believe what is said' means only an opinion of the truth of the saying. We should note, however, that the phrase 'I believe in,' as also the Latin Credo In and the Greek Pisteuo Eis, is never used outside the writings of divines. In other writings, the forms used are 'I believe him,' 'I have faith in him,' 'I rely on him,' and in Latin Credo Illi, Fido Illi, and in Greek Pisteuo Auto; and this peculiar ecclesiastical use of the phrase has raised many disputes about the proper object of the Christian faith.

But by 'believing in,' as in the Creed, what is meant is not trust in the person, but the confession and acknowledgement of the doctrine. For not only Christians, but men of every kind, do so believe in God, as to hold for true everything they hear him say, whether they understand it or not — which is all the faith and trust that can possibly be had in any person whatsoever; but they do not all believe the doctrine of the Creed.

From this we may conclude that whenever we believe a saying — of whatever kind — to be true, on the basis of arguments drawn not from the thing itself, nor from the principles of natural reason, but from the authority and good opinion we have of the one who said it, then the speaker, or the person we believe in or trust, and whose word we take, is the object of our faith; and the honour done in believing is done to him alone. Consequently, when we believe that the Scriptures are the word of God, having had no direct revelation from God himself, our belief, faith, and trust is in the Church, whose word we take and rest in. And those who believe what a prophet relates to them in the name of God take the prophet's word, do honour to him, and trust and believe in him concerning the truth of what he reports — whether he is a true prophet or a false one. The same goes for all other histories. If I did not believe everything that is written by historians about the glorious deeds of Alexander or Caesar, I do not think the ghost of Alexander or Caesar would have any just cause to be offended — nor anyone else, but the historian. If Livy says the gods once made a cow speak, and we do not believe it, we do not distrust God in this, but Livy. So it is plain that whatever we believe on no other ground than what is drawn from the authority of men only, and their writings, whether they were sent from God or not, is faith in men only.
